caption:
Optical imagery needs two things: sunlight and clear sky. During West Africa's rainy season, both disappear for weeks at a time — exactly when flood and pipeline risk peaks. That is a coverage gap, not a data problem.

Synthetic-aperture radar does not wait for either. It transmits its own energy and measures what bounces back. Cloud, smoke, and darkness do not block that signal the way they block a camera. The trade is resolution — radar reads texture and moisture, not fine detail — but it collects on schedule regardless of weather.

This is why revisit cadence and sensor mix matter more than headline resolution when the objective is early warning, not photography. A sharp image you cannot get during the event you care about is not a capability. It is a demo.
thread: Optical satellites need sunlight and clear sky. Rainy season strips away both — for weeks, in the exact window flood and pipeline risk peaks. That is a coverage gap.
Synthetic-aperture radar transmits its own energy and reads the backscatter. Cloud, smoke, darkness — none of it blocks the signal the way it blocks a camera.
The trade: radar resolution is coarser. It reads moisture and texture, not fine detail. For early warning that trade is usually correct. For forensic identification, it is not.
A sharp image you cannot collect during the event you're watching for isn't a capability. It's a demo.

card.headline: Cloud doesn't stop radar
card.sub: Optical needs sunlight and clear sky. Synthetic-aperture radar sends its own signal and reads what comes back — rain or shine, day or night.

rationale: Teaches the core optical-vs-radar mechanism in plain terms, directly relevant to rainy-season flood risk, without repeating prior revisit/quiet/resolution angles.
